title: How to Write a Movie Synopsis, With a Real Example
summary: Learn how to write a movie synopsis in 6 steps, from logline to one page, with the real synopsis of A Proper Introduction, a short film made in Flick.
body_markdown:
## What does a movie synopsis look like?


A synopsis is the story told plainly from start to finish, and the same film can carry three lengths of it: a one-sentence logline, a short paragraph and a one-page version.


### Logline (34 words)


A knight a few centimetres tall, imagined by a little girl, sets out to be introduced to her busy father, and learns that he has to find himself before anyone can really see him.


### Short synopsis (110 words)


Ser Loras is a knight a few centimetres tall, imagined by a girl named Lydia, and he has one task: to be introduced to her father. He crosses the yard and turns up in a cardboard box on the father's desk. The father studies him with care, but as a model to draw, and draws a helmet and armour that are not Loras at all. So Loras goes looking for himself, finds the crayon drawing Lydia made of him, and lays her drawings in a trail through the house before he crumbles into coloured dust. The father follows the drawings, and asks Lydia to tell him the knight's whole story.


### One-page synopsis (298 words)


Ser Loras is a knight a few centimetres tall, with a scroll case on his back and a sword and grappling hook at his belt. He has no surname, but he has a task: to be introduced to someone. He climbs over a windowsill and sets off across the grass.


Introductions matter more than they seem, he tells us, because until you are properly introduced you can be mistaken for all sorts of things. He drags a cardboard box to the front door, climbs inside, and is unpacked on the desk of a man whose wall is covered in drawings of armour and dragons.


For a while the plan seems to work. The man picks him up, looks at him with considerable care and draws him in pencil. But the drawing shows a helmet, a posture and a piece of armour, and Loras sees that it is not him.


He decides he must find himself first. In the bedroom of the man's daughter, Lydia, he reaches a drawer and pulls out the crayon drawing she made of him, half plain silver, half covered in pink flowers. She put it away there, promising to introduce him next time, when her dad was less busy.


But "next time" can become a place no one ever reaches. So Loras lays her drawings in a trail across the hall floor, sets down his scroll case, sword and hook, and crumbles into coloured dust.


Her father finds the drawings and follows them to her room, where the floor is covered in her pictures. When Lydia comes home, he is sitting on her bed with a stack of them, and asks her to tell him the knight's whole story. On the windowsill, Ser Loras sits on his drawing and watches the introduction finally happen.


More detail: how we read the film


We watched the finished film on its public[A Proper Introduction](https://flick.art/film/a-proper-introduction-4efa0c) page and read its burned-in narration, which is where the knight's lines in the one-page synopsis come from. Lydia's name, her promise to introduce him "next time, when Dad isn’t so busy" and her father's last question come from the shot prompts on the film's public canvas, read on 2026-10-30. The order of the beats and every sentence above are our reading of the film, not Jaime Yao's words; the director's own account of the story is in his post[Behind "Ser Loras"](https://flick.art/blog/behind-ser-loras) .
